content: Investing in early childhood development (ECD) is one of the most effective ways for a country to enhance shared prosperity, promote inclusive economic growth, expand equitable opportunities, and eradicate extreme poverty. This investment benefits governments, businesses, communities, parents, caregivers, and, most importantly, young children. It is not only a moral imperative, ensuring every child’s right to survive and thrive, but also a cost-effective strategy. For every dollar spent on ECD interventions, the return on investment can be as high as thirteen dollars. The period from pregnancy to age three is the most critical for brain development, as the brain grows faster during this time than at any other stage of life. By the age of three, 80% of a child’s brain is formed. For optimal brain development, children require a safe, secure, and loving environment, along with proper nutrition and stimulation provided by their parents or caregivers. This period represents a unique window of opportunity to establish a foundation for lifelong health and well-being, with benefits that extend into the next generation. The consequences of inaction are significant. Children who lack nurturing care in their early years are more likely to face learning difficulties in school, which can reduce their future earning potential and negatively impact the well-being and prosperity of their families and societies. Current estimates suggest that nearly 250 million children under the age of five in lowand middle-income countries—more than four in every ten—are at risk of missing critical developmental milestones due to poverty or stunting. The Nurturing Care Framework is based on the latest evidence on early childhood development and outlines the most effective policies and services to support parents and caregivers in providing nurturing care for their children. It serves as a roadmap for action, mobilizing a coalition of parents, caregivers, national governments, civil society groups, academics, the United Nations, the private sector, educational institutions, and service providers to ensure every child has the best start in life. The framework emphasizes the importance of universal health coverage, with primary care at its core, as essential for sustainable growth and development. It highlights the critical role of all sectors, including health, in supporting the healthy development of children to maximize their potential and benefit from pre-school and formal education. As we strive to achieve the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and ensure no one is left behind, it is imperative to prioritize investments in early childhood development at every level—national, community, and family. The framework provides strategic directions for supporting the holistic development of children from pregnancy to age three. It aims to inspire collaboration across multiple sectors, including health, nutrition, education, labor, finance, water and sanitation, and social and child protection, to address the needs of the youngest children. It underscores the importance of responsive caregiving and early learning as integral components of high-quality care for young children. Additionally, it demonstrates how existing programs can be enhanced to comprehensively address the needs of young children. The framework promotes the use of local resources, adaptation to local contexts, and community ownership. It outlines the foundations, actions, and government leadership required to ensure all children reach their full potential. It calls on policymakers, program managers, civil society groups, development partners, professional associations, academic institutions, and funding initiatives to work together to address gaps in support for the youngest children, complement the education sector’s efforts to improve pre-primary education, and ensure the material and social security of families and communities. The framework also highlights the unique role of the health sector in providing support for nurturing care during the earliest years, from pregnancy to age three. After this period, children transition into more formal preschool settings, where the education sector plays a pivotal role. The framework recognizes that optimal development results from interventions across various stages of life but focuses on the period from pregnancy to age three to leverage the health sector’s extensive reach and impact. The science of early childhood development has advanced significantly over the past three decades, with findings from various disciplines converging to demonstrate the profound impact of early experiences on children’s development. This knowledge underscores the urgency of addressing the needs of young children and their caregivers to ensure a brighter, more sustainable future for all.
